title: Curse of Dimensionality and Feature Extraction
abstract:
Adding features does not monotonically improve a model — past an optimal
number, performance degrades. This document explains why: exponential sparsity,
distance concentration, and the growth in the number of parameters that must be
estimated from a fixed sample. It derives the mathematics of each, demonstrates
the Hughes (peaking) phenomenon empirically, and sets up the solution the notes
give — dimensionality reduction, split into feature selection and feature
extraction (PCA, LDA, t-SNE) — which Topic 33 then works in full.

blocks.t: The Problem
From the notes

items:
Features $\to$ dimensions. Basically, the curse of
 features.

There is an optimal number of features; if we add more, the
 model would perform poorly.

With the increase of more features, sparsity between features
 increases, and not much relation stays between each feature, while
 computation increases.

Solution = Dimensionality Reduction $\rightarrow$
 Feature Selection and Feature Extraction (PCA, LDA,
 t-SNE).

blocks.t: Why more information can make things worse

It sounds contradictory: an extra column contains extra information, so how can
it hurt? Because a model does not receive information — it estimates
something from a finite sample. Every additional dimension spreads the same
number of rows over an exponentially larger space, so the amount of evidence
supporting any local estimate collapses. The information is there; the sample is
too small to extract it.
Cause 1 — Exponential Sparsity

blocks.cap:
Sixty points, three dimensionalities. Dividing each axis into five
 bins gives $5^d$ cells. In 1-D each cell holds a dozen points; in 3-D most
 cells are empty.

blocks.t: The arithmetic

Partition each of $d$ axes into $b$ bins. The number of cells is $b^d$, so the
expected occupancy is
\frac{n}{b^{d}} .

With $b=10$ and $n=10^6$: in 1-D each cell holds $10^5$ points; at $d=6$ it holds
one; at $d=10$ it holds $10^{-4}$ — one cell in ten thousand is occupied.

Turned around: to keep occupancy constant you need
$n \propto b^{d}$ — the sample size must grow exponentially in the
number of features. This is the curse of dimensionality in its original form.
The unit hypercube is almost all corner

Another way to see it. The volume of the unit ball inscribed in the unit cube in
$d$ dimensions is
V_d = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma \left(\tfrac d2+1\right)2^{d}} ,

which tends to $0$ as $d$ grows: $V_2=0.785$, $V_5=0.164$, $V_{10}=0.0025$. In
ten dimensions, 99.75% of the cube's volume lies outside the inscribed ball —
in the corners. "The middle of the data" effectively ceases to exist, and
almost every point is near a boundary.
Cause 2 — Distance Concentration

This is what the notes mean by "not much relation stays between each feature":
in high dimensions, all points become roughly equidistant.

blocks.cap:
Left: the ratio of the nearest to the farthest point from a query.
 At $d=1000$ it is essentially 1 — the nearest neighbour is no nearer than the
 farthest. Right: the relative spread of distances shrinks as $1/\sqrt{d}$.

blocks.t: Why distances concentrate

For i.i.d. components, the squared distance between two random points is a sum
of $d$ independent terms:

By the law of large numbers this sum concentrates around $d\,\mathbb{E}[(x_j-y_j)^2]$,
so $\|x-y\| \approx \sqrt{d}\,\sigma_0$ for every pair. The mean distance
grows as $\sqrt{d}$ while the standard deviation stays $O(1)$, giving
\frac{\operatorname{sd}(\|x-y\|)}{\mathbb{E}[\|x-y\|]}=O \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt d}\right)\longrightarrow 0 .
Beyer et al. (1999) proved the consequence:
\frac{d_{\max}-d_{\min}}{d_{\min}} \xrightarrow{ d\to\infty } 0 .
The concept of a "nearest neighbour" becomes meaningless.
Which algorithms this destroys

Anything built on distances: KNN (Topic 71), K-Means
(Topic 76), DBSCAN (Topic 78), SVM with an RBF kernel
(Topic 74), and the KNN imputer (Topic 26). All of them assume that
"close" means "similar", and in high dimensions nothing is close to anything.

Note that the concentration is driven by irrelevant dimensions. If only
three of your 500 features matter, the other 497 contribute pure noise to every
distance and drown the signal.
Cause 3 — Parameters to Estimate

With $n < d$ the design matrix is rank-deficient, $X^{\!\top}X$ is singular, and
OLS has no unique solution — the model can fit the training data perfectly and
means nothing. This is why regularisation (Topics 41–43) is not optional in
high dimensions.
The Peaking Phenomenon

blocks.cap:
Left: 300 rows, three genuinely informative features, and the rest
 pure noise. Accuracy rises to an optimal number of features and then
 falls — exactly as the notes describe. KNN degrades far faster than logistic
 regression, because it is distance-based. Right: the solution.

blocks.t: The Hughes phenomenon, 1968

For a fixed sample size, classifier accuracy increases with the number of
features up to an optimum and then decreases. The optimum grows with $n$
— with more data you can afford more features. This is the formal statement of
the notes' "there is an optimal number of features; if we add more, the model
would perform poorly".
The Solution
From the notes
Solution $=$ Dimensionality Reduction, which splits into:

items: Feature Selection — keep a subset of the original columns.

blocks.t: Why high-dimensional data is often reducible in practice

The curse describes the worst case: data filling the space uniformly. Real data
rarely does. A $784$-pixel MNIST image has 784 nominal dimensions, but handwritten
digits occupy a low-dimensional manifold inside that space — adjacent
pixels are correlated, and most of the $256^{784}$ possible images are noise, not
digits. This manifold hypothesis is why PCA on MNIST retains 95% of the
variance in about 150 components, and why dimensionality reduction works at all.
Code

import numpy as np, time
from scipy.special import gammaln
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, LassoCV
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. SPARSITY -- the sample size needed grows EXPONENTIALLY
# =====================================================================
print(f"{'d':>4s} {'cells (10 bins)':>18s} {'points/cell, n=1e6':>20s}")
for d in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20]:
    cells = 10.0 ** d
    print(f"{d:4d} {cells:18.2e} {1e6/cells:20.2e}")

# To keep 10 points per cell you would need n = 10 * 10^d rows:
for d in [5, 10, 20]:
    print(f"d={d:2d} needs n = {10 * 10.0**d:.1e} rows for 10 points per cell")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE HYPERCUBE IS ALMOST ALL CORNER
# =====================================================================
def ball_fraction(d):
    """Volume of the inscribed unit ball / volume of the unit cube."""
    return np.exp(d/2*np.log(np.pi) - gammaln(d/2 + 1) - d*np.log(2))

print(f"\n{'d':>4s} {'ball / cube':>14s} {'in the corners':>16s}")
for d in [2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50]:
    f = ball_fraction(d)
    print(f"{d:4d} {f:14.6f} {1-f:15.4%}")
# At d=10, 99.75% of the volume is in the corners. There is no "middle".

# =====================================================================
# 3. DISTANCE CONCENTRATION -- nearest stops meaning near
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'d':>5s} {'d_min':>8s} {'d_max':>8s} {'min/max':>9s} {'sd/mean':>9s}")
for d in [1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000]:
    X = rng.uniform(0, 1, (1000, d))
    q = rng.uniform(0, 1, (1, d))
    dist = np.sqrt(((X - q) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    print(f"{d:5d} {dist.min():8.3f} {dist.max():8.3f} "
          f"{dist.min()/dist.max():9.3f} {dist.std()/dist.mean():9.4f}")
# min/max -> 1.0 and sd/mean -> 0: every point is the same distance away.

# =====================================================================
# 4. IT IS THE IRRELEVANT DIMENSIONS THAT DO THE DAMAGE
# =====================================================================
n = 500
signal = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 3))
y = (signal[:, 0] + .7*signal[:, 1] - .5*signal[:, 2] + rng.normal(0, .4, n) > 0).astype(int)

print(f"\n{'total features':>15s} {'KNN':>8s} {'LogReg':>8s} {'Forest':>8s}")
for d in [3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 300, 800]:
    X = np.c_[signal, rng.normal(0, 1, (n, max(d-3, 0)))]      # noise columns
    k = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(5), X, y, cv=5).mean()
    l = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=800), X, y, cv=5).mean()
    f = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100,
                                               random_state=0), X, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{d:15d} {k:8.3f} {l:8.3f} {f:8.3f}")
# The SIGNAL is unchanged throughout -- only noise columns were added.
# KNN collapses fastest (distance-based). Forests resist best (they select).

# =====================================================================
# 5. n < d -- the design matrix becomes singular
# =====================================================================
for n_, d_ in [(200, 50), (200, 200), (200, 500)]:
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_, d_))
    print(f"n={n_:4d} d={d_:4d}  rank {np.linalg.matrix_rank(X):4d}  "
          f"cond(X'X) {np.linalg.cond(X.T @ X):.2e}")
# Once d >= n the matrix is rank-deficient: infinitely many perfect fits,
# none of which generalise. Regularisation (Topics 41-43) is mandatory.

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE SOLUTION -- selection vs extraction, measured
# =====================================================================
X = np.c_[signal, rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 297))]        # 300 features, 3 real
base = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=800))
print(f"\nall 300 features         : "
      f"{cross_val_score(base, X, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")

# FEATURE SELECTION -- keeps ORIGINAL columns, stays interpretable
sel = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=5),
                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=800))
print(f"selection, k=5           : {cross_val_score(sel, X, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")

chosen = SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=5).fit(X, y).get_support(indices=True)
print(f"  columns kept: {chosen}  (the true signal is 0,1,2)")

# FEATURE EXTRACTION -- builds NEW columns
ext = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=5),
                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=800))
print(f"PCA, 5 components        : {cross_val_score(ext, X, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")

# LDA is SUPERVISED, and capped at C-1 components
lda = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=1),
                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=800))
print(f"LDA, 1 component (C-1=1) : {cross_val_score(lda, X, y, cv=5).mean():.3f}")

# EMBEDDED selection -- Lasso drives irrelevant coefficients to exactly zero
las = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=0).fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), y)
print(f"Lasso kept {np.sum(las.coef_ != 0)} of {X.shape[1]} features; "
      f"the true 3 are among them: {set(range(3)) <= set(np.flatnonzero(las.coef_))}")

# NOTE: unsupervised PCA can discard the signal, because maximum variance
# is not the same as maximum relevance. That is exactly what LDA fixes.

# =====================================================================
# 7. COMPUTATION INCREASES -- the notes' other claim
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'d':>6s} {'KNN fit+predict':>18s} {'LogReg fit':>13s}")
for d in [10, 100, 1000, 3000]:
    X_ = rng.normal(0, 1, (3000, d)); y_ = rng.integers(0, 2, 3000)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    KNeighborsClassifier(5).fit(X_[:2000], y_[:2000]).predict(X_[2000:])
    tk = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter()
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=200).fit(X_, y_)
    tl = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f"{d:6d} {tk:17.3f}s {tl:12.3f}s")

# =====================================================================
# 8. THE MANIFOLD HYPOTHESIS -- why reduction works in practice
# =====================================================================
t = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, 2000)                     # ONE intrinsic dimension
X_manifold = np.c_[np.cos(t), np.sin(t), 0.5*np.cos(2*t)]
X_manifold = X_manifold @ rng.normal(0, 1, (3, 200))  # embedded in 200-D
X_manifold += rng.normal(0, .01, X_manifold.shape)

p = PCA().fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_manifold))
cum = np.cumsum(p.explained_variance_ratio_)
print(f"\nnominal dimensions: {X_manifold.shape[1]}")
print(f"components for 95% variance: {np.searchsorted(cum, .95) + 1}")
print(f"components for 99% variance: {np.searchsorted(cum, .99) + 1}")
# 200 nominal dimensions, ~3 real ones. Real data is like this far more often
# than the worst case the curse describes.
Worked Examples
Why more features make data sparse
Draw points uniformly in the unit cube $[0,1]^d$. Call the inner region $[0.1,0.9]^d$ the "core". A point lies in the core with probability
P(\text{core}) = (0.8)^d
because each coordinate independently has probability $0.8$ of landing in $[0.1,0.9]$.

Reading it. In 100 dimensions almost every point sits in the outer shell. Neighbours are far apart, distance-based methods (KNN, K-Means) lose meaning, and the number of samples needed to cover the space grows exponentially. That is the curse of dimensionality, and it is the motivation for feature selection and extraction.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Features $\to$ dimensions — the curse of dimensionality is the
 curse of features.

There is an optimal number of features; adding more makes the
 model perform poorly. This is the Hughes or
 peaking phenomenon.

Cause 1 — sparsity. With $b$ bins per axis there are $b^d$
 cells, so the sample size needed grows exponentially. At $d=10$,
 99.75% of a unit cube's volume is in its corners.

Cause 2 — distance concentration. Distances grow as
 $\sqrt{d}$ while their spread stays $O(1)$, so
 $(d_{\max}-d_{\min})/d_{\min}\to0$: not much relation stays
 between each feature. This destroys KNN, K-Means, DBSCAN, RBF-SVM.

Cause 3 — parameters. Once $d\ge n$ the design matrix is
 singular and OLS has no unique solution.
Computation increases with $d$ for every algorithm.

Solution = Dimensionality Reduction:
 Feature Selection (keep a subset of original columns,
 interpretable) and Feature Extraction (PCA, LDA,
 t-SNE — new synthetic columns).

PCA is unsupervised and linear; LDA is supervised and capped at $C-1$
 components; t-SNE is non-linear and for visualisation only.

Real data usually lies on a low-dimensional manifold, which is
 why reduction works despite the worst-case theory.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What is the curse of dimensionality?

As the number of features grows, the volume of the space grows exponentially, so
a fixed sample becomes exponentially sparse. Distances concentrate — every point
becomes roughly equidistant from every other — and the number of parameters to
estimate grows while the evidence per parameter shrinks. Past an optimum, adding
features makes the model worse.
Q. Why does it hurt KNN more than a random forest?

KNN's entire mechanism is distance, and distance concentration destroys it
directly: with 300 features of which three matter, the 297 irrelevant ones drown
the signal in every distance computation. A forest evaluates one feature at a
time and effectively performs selection, so irrelevant columns are largely
ignored.
Q. If more information is better, how can adding a feature hurt?

Because the model estimates from a finite sample. An extra dimension spreads the
same rows over an exponentially larger space, so the evidence supporting any
estimate collapses. The information exists; the sample is too small to exploit
it, and the extra parameter adds variance.
Q. Feature selection or feature extraction?

Selection when you must explain the model — the surviving columns are still
"age" and "income". Extraction when you want maximum compression and can
tolerate synthetic components. Selection discards whatever information the
dropped columns held; extraction combines information from all of them.
Q. Why might PCA hurt a supervised model?

Because PCA is unsupervised: it maximises variance, and the direction of greatest
variance need not be the direction that separates the classes. A low-variance
component can carry all the signal and be discarded. LDA fixes this by maximising
class separation instead — but is limited to $C-1$ components.
Q. MNIST images have 784 pixels. Is that 784 real dimensions?

No. Digits lie on a low-dimensional manifold inside pixel space — adjacent
pixels are highly correlated and almost every point in the space is noise rather
than a digit. PCA retains 95% of the variance in roughly 150 components. This
manifold structure is why dimensionality reduction works in practice despite the
worst-case theory.
